title: Child among three dead in Russian nightly strikes near Kyiv
description: At least three people, including a child, have been killed in overnight Russian attacks near the Ukrainian capital Kyiv.In the early hours of Saturday
body: At least three people, including a child, have been killed in overnight Russian attacks near the Ukrainian capital Kyiv.In the early hours of Saturday missiles hit east of the capital and witnesses reported hearing powerful explosions just days after strikes across Ukraine killed 21 people.Falling debris damaged apartment buildings and cars, while a fire broke out at a separate building, the head of the regional military administration Timur Tkachenko said. He added that three others had been wounded in the ballistic missile strikes.Emergency crews were also fighting fires at a building and fuel tank in Kyiv, Mayor Vitaly Klitchko wrote on Telegram.Ukraine's state emergency service DSNS shared photos showing garages, a business and a building on fire in Kyiv, adding: "The number of victims is being clarified."President Volodymyr Zelensky has arrived in Serbia for his first visit after raising concerns about Ukraine's capacity to fend off Russian missile attacks due to depleting interceptors stockpiles.Earlier in the week, Zelensky said delays in receiving anti-ballistic systems from partners leads to "horrific casualties and destruction", saying that having a stronger interceptor capability "could have saved lives" in recent deadly assaults.The president later said the supply of interceptors from allies had been "significantly reduced" this year.It came after Ukraine hit two oil refineries deep inside Russia along with Moscow-linked vessels in the Black Sea, which Zelensky said was intended to limit oil revenues used by Russia to "finance" its war in Ukraine.Recent mediation talks have faltered, leading to an escalation of attacks between both sides.

schema.headline: Child among three dead in Russian nightly strikes near Kyiv

title: Footballer Ivan Toney charged with assault at Soho nightclub
description: England footballer Ivan Toney has been charged with assault at a nightclub in central London.The 30-year-old, who plays for Saudi Pro League club Al-A
body: England footballer Ivan Toney has been charged with assault at a nightclub in central London.The 30-year-old, who plays for Saudi Pro League club Al-Ahli, was charged on 31 July following an incident on Wardour Street in Soho on 6 December.The former Brentford striker, who started England's 6-4 win over France in the "bronze final" of the World Cup last month, has been charged with assault causing actual bodily harm and is due to appear at Westminster Magistrates' Court on 24 September.A spokesperson for Toney said: "Ivan acknowledges the charge and although he is naturally shocked, he looks forward to being given the opportunity to clear his name in court."After starting his career at Northampton Town, the striker had permanent spells at Newcastle, Peterborough and Brentford before moving to Saudi Arabia in 2024.He was a surprise selection for England's World Cup squad but apart from the France game, his only other appearance was as a late substitute in the 2-1 semi-final defeat to Argentina.

schema.headline: Footballer Ivan Toney charged with assault at Soho nightclub

title: Digital cameras and wired earphones are back - and 'a bit more real'
description: Luckily I'm out with my photography-loving best friend, who helps adjust the settings on the camera and gets snapping while I'm otherwise engaged on t
body: Luckily I'm out with my photography-loving best friend, who helps adjust the settings on the camera and gets snapping while I'm otherwise engaged on the dancefloor.The mere sight of us pulling out the camera and squinting through its tiny viewfinder draws attention – "I've not seen one of these in years", a man remarks.He's right – digital cameras had their heyday in the late 1990s and early 2000s, just before smartphones took off.There are currently 42 million active film camera users globally, more than a third of these aged 18–30 and largely influenced by social media trends, according to a market research report, external last year.So why, when we're surrounded by more advanced tech here in 2026, are they seemingly making a resurgence?For Lily Redman, a 26-year-old content creator from South Wales, digital cameras "capture a quality that my phone just can't replicate".She's been taking one on nights out and to concerts and feels the flash on her phone "is grainy and too high definition" compared to the "more smooth" finished product on a digital camera."I think people are looking for a bit of grit or something that feels a bit more real," she says.That may also explain why low exposure photos taken on iPhones and Androids – where people dodge ready-made filters to artificially crank down the exposure setting and produce a darker image – are also popular on socials right now.With digital cameras offering an element of surprise when you plug in the memory card reader to your computer at home, digital cameras capture a moment in time."If I look back at photos my mum took when I was two, they look so old but when I look at photos I took five years ago, they look like they were taken yesterday," says Redman. "Phone photos have warped our perception of time."It's not just digital cameras returning from the archives (or a dusty cupboard), but early MP3 devices like iPods too.According to refurbished tech website Backmarket, iPods are "driving the trend" in sales of older MP3 devices with a 48% increase in sales between 2024 and 2025, with demand for MP3 and MP4 players "accelerating further into 2026".Cheri Sanih, 30, runs a Tumblr account about older technology which she says has gained thousands of followers recently.As she scrolls through the music library on her mint green iPod, filled with album artwork from 15 to 20 years ago, childhood memories of receiving one as a Christmas present come flooding back.For her, it's all about nostalgically "wanting to remember simpler times"; being able to "bury into escapism".Sanih points out how her "phone is always getting notifications and sometimes I just want to be outside, blissfully listening to music".She thinks iPods have become popular again because of their "beautiful design" and the way the music player is "the first bit of technology really catering to humans with a less cluttered user interface".And speaking of back to basics, wired headphones are perhaps as simple as you can get, but again proving popular online.These are now a daily staple for 23-year-old Monique Wellman-Mason from Bristol, who grew tired of losing her wireless earbuds."Every single time I get them out my bag I spend two minutes trying to detangle them which is a bit of a pain," she jokes, "but at the same time I love that they have a microphone and I'm [always] connected to my phone".She tells the BBC that the clear mic is useful for her job as a social media manager and she enjoys being able to "spark that nostalgia", while another positive is wired earphones are "really cheap" at about £20.Monique made the switch from bluetooth wireless to wired earphones a few months back and says she hasn't returned to the former since. "Technology only goes up and we're always looking for the quickest thing but this is a step back in a way – I love it," she says.Whether it's digital cameras, iPods or wired earphones, does a renewed love for early-digital gadgets among some young people tell us something more?It's been on the mind of Andrew Przybylski, professor of technology and human behaviour at the University of Oxford.Underpinning a fondness for more basic tech is "people's desire on a very deep level to be in control of their experiences," he argues.He says the modern digital world often leaves us inflicted by decision paralysis, external - the inability to choose because there are so many options.When a new series comes out, he explains, "binge watching it automatically" often feels like a decision that is made for us.In contrast, when you choose to turn on a digital camera and play with its settings or add an album to your iPod library "you move towards something you want versus it coming at you".Andrew says "people want more than to just rent the things [and experiences] they're passionate about" and that buying your own music or taking your own pictures creates a sense of connection.He references Xbox's server outage in late July, in which users couldn't play games even if they owned the discs and how "nobody liked that"."Imagine if a book worked that way," he adds.Additional reporting by Amy Walker.

schema.headline: Digital cameras and wired earphones are back - and 'a bit more real'

title: Katseye singer Sophia Laforteza steps away from group over mental health
description: The label said Laforteza has been receiving "the utmost support" and consulting medical professionals, and has been advised to dedicate time to "exten
body: The label said Laforteza has been receiving "the utmost support" and consulting medical professionals, and has been advised to dedicate time to "extended rest and ongoing care to ensure a full recovery"."While Sophia herself is eager to perform alongside her members, the health, safety, and long-term well-being of our artists will always remain our highest priority," the statement said, noting that her condition will be reassessed in September.In a separate statement, Laforteza wrote on Instagram: "Making this decision wasn't easy, but I'm learning that health has to come first. I'm realizing that if I don't take care of my mind and body now, I won't be able to keep doing what I love the most for so long."She added: "It means more to me than I could ever say. I promise I'm going to work as hard as I can to get through this, heal properly, and come back stronger."The girl group formed with six members in 2023 and was nominated for two Grammy Awards last year. It now will continue events with four members. The group has previously said its members have received multiple online death threats since they made their debut.In February, the label announced that Katseye member Bannerman would take a temporary break to focus on her health and wellbeing, as well. She has not returned but their label has said the door will always be open. The 23-year-old Swiss singer told fans she was "healthy" and "taking care of myself".The group said the decision had been made following "open and thoughtful conversations together".

schema.headline: Katseye singer Sophia Laforteza steps away from group over mental health

title: Book hidden in fireplace returned to Australian library 150 years overdue
description: Image source, Kiama CouncilImage caption, A former apprentice stonemason who helped build the Houses of Parliament is thought to have borrowed the boo
body: Image source, Kiama CouncilImage caption, A former apprentice stonemason who helped build the Houses of Parliament is thought to have borrowed the book in the late 1800sByLana LamSydneyA book borrowed 150 years ago has finally been returned to an Australian library, with the culprit linked to the Houses of Parliament in London.Antiquities of Athens was borrowed from a local library in Kiama, a seaside town about 120km (75 miles) south of Sydney, some time in the mid-1870s.The book on classic Greek architecture was stored in a tea chest hidden behind a boarded-up fireplace for decades before it was recently discovered by a family member.Ross Simmons, 77, thinks his great-grandfather, John Simmons, might have borrowed the book to help with his career, having worked as an apprentice stonemason in Westminster in the mid-1800s before becoming an architect in Australia.Image source, Kiama CouncilImage caption, The book was a little water damaged but otherwise in a good conditionSimmons, a self-confessed family history buff, said his great-grandfather studied in London between 1839 to 1844."After his studies in London, he was apprenticed to other stonemasons to help in the construction of the Houses of Parliament," Simmons said.In 1857, aged 27, John Simmons emigrated from the UK to Australia, first living in the Sydney suburb of Newtown before relocating to Kiama after leading the construction of a sandstone church in the coastal town."He had quite an interest in architecture, construction and building," Simmons said, adding that the overdue book "probably sat on a shelf at his house" and was used as a reference.The book somehow ended up in a tea chest - along with other family records - which was placed in a fireplace that was covered up.Image source, Supplied: Jo HartmannImage caption, The fireplace where the book was found had been sealed for decadesAbout 30 years ago, the tea chest was uncovered during renovations and the books - including the overdue one - were given to Simmons for safekeeping.But it wasn't until about a fortnight ago that he went through some of the books in greater detail."I looked inside the front cover and, lo and behold, on the second page there was a Kiama Library stamp," Simmons said, with the library's borrowing conditions also detailed on the inside cover.For instance, library members could only borrow one book at a time, unless it could be proved that six people in the same household could read, in which case, three books could be lent out.Anyone intoxicated was barred from borrowing and members returning books past their due date would be fined three pence for every week it was late.Kiama Library staff worked out that the fine would be £97 - or in today's currency  AU$28,000 ($20,000; £15,000), allowing for inflation. But luckily for the Simmons family, the fine has been waived.Kiama Council libraries manager Michelle Hudson said the unusual find had attracted a lot of attention.Image source, Jane ThompsonImage caption, Kiama Council libraries manager Michelle Hudson said people have travelled from out of town to come and see the book"People have travelled 40 minutes away to come and actually hold the book... it's a beautiful little book and it's got an amazing story to tell," she said.The cloth-bound volume has some water damage but otherwise, is in good condition, Hudson said."It does have beautiful illustrations in it and some pages that fold out to show you they were using exact measurements of some of the monuments in Greece."She said in 1872, the council got a £200 grant to establish the town's library and and it had fewer than 1,000 books in its collection, with the overdue book marked as number 506.Image source, Catherine TaylorImage caption, The book, published in 1858, features Greek monument illustrations that fold outThere's no way to know exactly who borrowed the book or when, Hudson said, as the library's borrowing records from that period have since been lost.However, the book is no longer available to borrow, having been added to the library's collection of special items, which can be viewed on request. "It won't be able to go out again... we don't want to wait another 150 years for it to come back," Hudson joked.As for the book's much-delayed return, Simmons said he believes his great-grandfather would be pleased with the final chapter of its journey."I think he'd be happy to see the book returned and he'd probably have a bit of a laugh about it."Image source, Kiama LibraryImage caption, The book was borrowed from the library which was housed in this building from 1872 to 1890

schema.headline: Book hidden in fireplace returned to Australian library 150 years overdue

title: Appeals court halts Trump's ballroom project paving way for Supreme Court showdown
description: "Congress has not ceded unfettered authority to the Executive Branch to dramatically redesign, reshape, and reconstruct the White House — the People's
body: "Congress has not ceded unfettered authority to the Executive Branch to dramatically redesign, reshape, and reconstruct the White House — the People's ​House — to fit a particular President's desires," the panel said.The three-judge panel, in a 2-1 decision, said: "Each President is a temporary tenant, not the owner, of the White House and its Executive Residence.""The President has no - and claims no - constitutionally assigned authority over that property, which is designed and maintained for the use of all Presidents, current and future, and for the American people," the opinion said.The administration appealed to the court after a federal judge twice blocked above-ground construction on the ballroom, while still allowing underground work to proceed.The ruling on Friday upholds the order blocking above-ground construction without congressional approval. The appeals court delayed implementation of its ruling for 14 days to allow the Trump administration to appeal to the Supreme Court.The BBC has contacted the White House and Department of Justice for comment. Trump railed against the "horrendous" and "politically motivated" decision on social media, highlighting the dissenting judge's opinion that the order is "a blatant abuse of discretion".He said the military and Secret Service viewed the ruling as a national security threat."This unjust decision must be overturned by the Supreme Court in its entirety," he wrote.He also repeated that the ballroom was being built ahead of schedule and under budget, as a gift to the American people funded by a coalition of private donors.However, Republicans have sought to use a portion of $1bn (£740m) in taxpayer funds for Secret Service security upgrades - a plan that was brushed aside by a budget watchdog in May.President Trump has asserted that the new ballroom is needed to "accommodate people for grand parties, State Visits", and has also said that it is "vital for National Security".The ballroom building would consist of the large entertaining space above ground and also a security complex below ground. Trump doubled down on the need for the space after an assassination attempt at the White House Correspondents' Association dinner in April.The National Trust for Historic Preservation celebrated the ruling on Friday, noting that no above-ground construction can take place "unless and until" Congress takes action."The White House, a global landmark that symbolizes American identity and the ideals of democracy, belongs to the American people," said Brent Leggs, President and CEO of the National Trust."The National Trust for Historic Preservation and its partners are proud to defend this irreplaceable monument on behalf of all Americans."Trump has touted the ballroom project repeatedly since he unveiled plans for it in July 2025. It would have been the most substantial structural change to the presidential residence in more than 70 years.But the project has been mired in legal issues since October, when the Trump administration demolished the East Wing, which was built in 1902, to begin construction. Trump initially said the project would be "near" the East Wing, not that it would be demolished.Government lawyers have argued the additional security complex and features included in the ballroom project are needed to protect the White House complex from drones, ballistic missiles, biohazards and other threats - changes essential to protecting the president, his family, and staff. Trump said on Friday that construction includes bomb shelters, hospital and medical facilities and top secret military facilities. But the Trust said there was no basis to "disturb" the White House and argued that having a ballroom isn't a national security emergency.The three-judge appeals court panel said on Friday that its ruling "has nothing at all to do with whether the proposed ballroom is desirable", nor does it weigh in on whether the administration may ultimately construct the ballroom. "What it does mean is that the Defendants may not do so during the district court's expeditious litigation without securing Congress's authorization, as the Constitution and laws require," the order said.

schema.headline: Appeals court halts Trump's ballroom project paving way for Supreme Court showdown

title: Gianni Infantino denies claims Uefa paid off alleged 'lover'
description: Gianni Infantino's alleged lover was given a severance payment over the affair by Uefa while he was its general secretary, according to a Daily Telegr
body: Gianni Infantino's alleged lover was given a severance payment over the affair by Uefa while he was its general secretary, according to a Daily Telegraph investigation, external.A spokesman for the now Fifa president was reported to have told the paper Infantino "strongly denies these categorically untrue allegations".Uefa, for whom Infantino was general secretary from 2009 to 2016, issued a statement confirming "a departure payment was made to the individual in question".The allegations come as Infantino fights for his future as Fifa president following his aborted plans to sell off stakes in the World Cup to private investors.BBC Sport has contacted Fifa and Infantino for comment.The Telegraph reported that Uefa paid a six-figure sum to the woman, who had an alleged relationship with Infantino, who is married, during his time at European football's governing body."Fifa president Gianni Infantino strongly denies these allegations, and they are categorically untrue. Any insinuation of inappropriate conduct or violation of statutes or regulations is defamatory," a Fifa spokesman told the Telegraph."No employee at Uefa and Fifa has ever raised a complaint regarding Mr Infantino's behaviour because there never was an incident where he was involved."Uefa confirmed a payment was made to the woman in question and that it covered the fees for her to complete an MBA course at a local business school. It said all payments were in line with regulations at the time, but those regulations have since been tightened and "reflect those found in a modern, high-profile organisation".

schema.headline: Gianni Infantino denies claims Uefa paid off alleged 'lover'

title: 'Sex predator let out to kill' and 'net zero plans rolled back'
description: Several front pages carry pictures of the killer and rapist, Simon Levy, and the women he murdered. The Daily Express says he's "likely to die behind
body: Several front pages carry pictures of the killer and rapist, Simon Levy, and the women he murdered. The Daily Express says he's "likely to die behind bars", external following his conviction yesterday. The Daily Mail describes him as a "Tube Monster", referencing his attacks on the London Underground network. In an article for the paper, the Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch calls Levy a "modern-day Jack the Ripper", external, and argues a tougher criminal justice system is needed to protect people.The Daily Telegraph says Andy Burnham is considering an "about turn" on blocking the early prison release of two of PC Andrew Harper's killers, external. The Sun quotes a government source as saying the PM is prepared to "explore every option"., externalThe new energy secretary has told the Times that the government could relax some of Labour's net zero targets, external to help reduce the cost of living. Miatta Fahnbulleh tells the paper that ministers won't stick rigidly to a pledge to nearly eliminate fossil fuels from Britain's power supplies by 2030 – if doing so would risk higher household bills.According to the Daily Telegraph, European football's governing body paid off a member of staff – who it claims was an alleged mistress of Gianni Infantino – when he was Uefa's general secretary., external The organisation he now leads, Fifa, tells the paper that Infantino strongly denies the allegations, and that there have never been any complaints by employees about his behaviour. The Telegraph said Uefa had admitted a payment had been made, which it said had been in accordance with regulations at the time, and that those rules had since been tightened.The Guardian casts doubt on the stereotype that holidaying Germans hog sun loungers. It highlights a poll of European tourists by YouGov, that suggests the Italians and the French are more likely to reserve a spot with a towel, external. According to the paper, the British are the least likely to hog a sun lounger.

schema.headline: 'Sex predator let out to kill' and 'net zero plans rolled back'

title: Uefa boycott: France set to compete at U20 Women's World Cup
description: France say they are still planning to compete in the Under-20 Women's World Cup next month despite a threat from Uefa to boycott Fifa competitions.It
body: France say they are still planning to compete in the Under-20 Women's World Cup next month despite a threat from Uefa to boycott Fifa competitions.It is not known whether England will play or not, with the Football Association unable to provide a comment when asked by BBC Sport if the team will take part in the tournament in Poland, which is due to start in 29 days.After Fifa president Gianni Infantino announced a plan to sell stakes in competitions to private investors, European football's 55 member associations voted to boycott all Fifa competitions until the proposals were dropped.The plans have since been aborted - with Infantino apologising for his "errors".In a statement on Thursday, Uefa said the boycott could still go ahead, but when contacted by BBC Sport the French Football Federation (FFF) said its plans for the tournament had not changed."For now, France will be participating to the Fifa U20 Women World Cup," it said.Six European teams - England, France, Italy, Portugal, Spain and hosts Poland - are scheduled to play in the tournament.Women's football would be the first to be significantly impacted if Uefa's stance is upheld:5 September: Women's Under-20 World Cup due to startOctober: England, Northern Ireland, Scotland, Wales and the Republic of Ireland all have qualifiers for next summer's Women's World Cup in BrazilOctober: The Under-17 Women's World Cup is scheduled to take place in MoroccoJune 2027:  Should they not feature in the play-offs because of Uefa's boycott, European teams - including defending champions Spain - would not be able to participate in the Women's World Cup

schema.headline: Uefa boycott: France set to compete at U20 Women's World Cup

title: This Olympian curbed his unhealthy porn habit - here are the signs and steps to recovery
description: Former Team GB diver Freddie Woodward was a teenager when he realised he had a problem with porn."Every time I sat down to revise, all I wanted to do
body: Former Team GB diver Freddie Woodward was a teenager when he realised he had a problem with porn."Every time I sat down to revise, all I wanted to do was open those sites," he revealed.By age 12, he was regularly visiting what he calls "hardcore" sites. As his career progressed - which included representing his country in the Olympics - he was watching adult content several times a day.Now aged 30, the Olympian has told the BBC how he eventually curbed his habit by shifting his mindset."You can't be the person who is trying to quit porn. You have to be someone who doesn't watch porn, and that takes a lot of work," he said. So how can you spot when a porn habit has become unhealthy, and how can you tackle it?Although it has become a common phrase, "porn addiction" is not an officially recognised condition in its own right. "We know a lot of people have a problem with porn," explains sex and relationship psychotherapist Silva Neves, who says the matter has become more prevalent among clients at his private practice.But experts are divided as to whether it is a true "addiction" – like someone might experience with drugs, for example – and how best to deal with it.Researcher Campbell Ince, from Australia's Monash University, says the vast majority of clinicians now agree people can suffer from "problematic porn use", but there is still a lot to figure out about its causes and treatments.This means there is no definitive list of symptoms or treatments available to those worried they may be addicted.Some clinicians approach it as a compulsive sexual behaviour disorder, a condition recognised by the World Health Organization.This is sexual behaviour that "feels out of control, is causing significant distress, and despite repeated attempts to control it, they can't," explains psychotherapist Dr Paula Hall, who works privately at the Laurel Centre, a sex and porn addiction centre, and also runs a not-for-profit service.The NHS does say, external it is possible to be addicted to "just about anything", including sex.So what are the markers of an unhealthy porn habit? Neves says it's "not about the frequency or duration, it's about the damage to your life". That might be arriving late to work because you were up all night watching porn, prioritising it above commitments to your loved ones, or watching it in the office, he says.Other crucial questions to ask yourself are whether you can actually cut back or adjust your habit when you try, and whether you carry on watching despite enjoying it less and less, adds Ince, whose research focuses on problematic porn use.For Craig, who describes himself as a recovering addict, it was this loss of control which marked a turning point during the Covid-19 pandemic, when he was in his mid-thirties."I don't think it ever became a huge issue for me until lockdown, where that extra pressure, extra isolation, just compounded the issue."I didn't know how to get it to loosen its grip on me," he recalls.Ince cautions that many people may feel distress about their porn use for social, moral or religious reasons – but that this does not necessarily mean your habit is out of control."Someone could be watching porn for five minutes, three times a week – and because they have a lot of shame, they think 'I'm an addict'," agrees Neves."But then there might be someone who watches it every day and thinks it's fine."Hall similarly encourages clients to "get away from the idea of 'I'm either an addict or I'm not'", and focus instead on how much it is affecting things like your studies and relationships.TV presenter Ore Oduba last year spoke publicly about his 30-year-long porn addiction which began at the age of nine – saying it had been "destroying my life from the inside out"."It was the thing from a very early age that I was running to as a response to a lot of trauma", he told the We Need to Talk podcast last year, before curbing the habit.It is not clear what might cause such behaviour, as experts say much more research is needed."The scientific examination is certainly accelerating, but there is a very long way to go," Ince says.It might begin as something which gives you a break from other issues in your life, says Hall, such as a stressful career or relationship breakdown.There may also be "predisposing factors", such as trauma, issues from early childhood, or negative self-belief, that can make it harder to curb your use, she says.Craig, now 40, says porn became a "tool to turn to for every one of life's ups and downs".He remembers feeling he was "broken, that there was no way out", before recovery helped him to think differently.Hall also points to the impact of the digital environment and people becoming "addicted by design" through algorithms.Both she and Neves say AI-generated porn is making matters worse by enabling people to create "exactly what they want and need", as Neves describes it.If you are worried about your porn use, Ince recommends seeking out support from a qualified and experienced professional.A registered psychologist can be particularly helpful because they may consider your mental health more broadly, "and we know that co-occurring mental health problems are more or less the rule, rather than the exception", he says.This was the case for Craig, who did not realise his porn use may be unhealthy until he started therapy for his mental health."Porn addiction was like a contributing factor," he came to learn.His therapist suggested he join a 12-step programme for sex addiction – a recovery model created by Alcoholics Anonymous – which he credits for his recovery."I didn't necessarily find it easy and straightforward to step away from my addiction. I feel I'm in a good place now, but also acknowledge the fact it's one day at a time."There is currently no central, dedicated NHS service for those struggling with their porn use – although some local services offer support, and you can talk to your GP. This means treatment will more likely come from private practitioners, support groups or online self-help.Ince suggests doing thorough research to find the right fit for you, and cautions against using online resources which may offer generic advice.Some practitioners will help clients towards cutting out porn altogether, while others will help people "integrate it into their lives in a way that is functional," says Neves. Seeking to understand any underlying factors will be a crucial part of treatment, says Hall.There are some practical steps you can take yourself, she says, such as placing blocking software on your device.She also advises recognising when you might feel more susceptible to using porn – which, for some, can be when you are stressed or alone – and planning ahead for what you might do instead.But she says there should ultimately be more support on the NHS, particularly early intervention before porn can take over a person's life.A spokesperson for the Department of Health and Social Care said: "It is troubling to hear accounts of individuals becoming addicted to pornography at such a young age."It reinforces the importance of the online safety laws we have put in place to prevent children from accessing harmful content."

schema.headline: This Olympian curbed his unhealthy porn habit - here are the signs and steps to recovery

title: Cambridge to review process for hiring senior academics after Jason Arday resignation
description: The University of Cambridge will review its process for appointing senior academics following the resignation of Jason Arday in the midst of a plagiar
body: The University of Cambridge will review its process for appointing senior academics following the resignation of Jason Arday in the midst of a plagiarism row.The institution said findings from an investigation into the education professor's academic qualifications and appointments would "feed into" a new review on the appointment process for senior academic roles.The Jesus College fellow has also faced accusations of fabricating or exaggerating elements of his CV. He has defended himself and his work, with attention now turning to Cambridge's handling of concerns and his upcoming memoir.News of the review comes after a group of academics called for an independent probe into his appointment.Priyamvada Gopal, professor of postcolonial studies at Cambridge and among those calling for an independent inquiry, said the university was facing "massive reputational damage" over the affair."This is reputational damage that has upset colleagues across disciplines, across the political spectrum," she told BBC Radio 4's Today programme on Friday."I've been quite struck by the number of people who are very upset by what has happened. So I don't think it is an option for Cambridge to just sweep this under the carpet and not take any action at all."Gopal said the university should not be "marking its own homework", adding that the group of academics of which she is a part had suggested a mix of senior academics at Cambridge and elsewhere to conduct an investigation.Cambridge said on Friday that it was "fully aware of the public commentary and concerns" and would "continue to investigate the circumstances around Jason Arday's appointment and tenure". A spokesperson declined to comment further.It previously announced an investigation into "new information" about Arday's academic qualifications and appointments on Wednesday, having already said it was looking into allegations of plagiarism.Jesus College welcomed the appointments review, saying Arday's role as fellow there had been "contingent on his university position"."We rely on the university to do checks on academic credentials for its appointments," a spokeswoman added.The University of Glasgow, where Arday worked for just over a year before moving to Cambridge, has commissioned its own review of his appointment."Jason Arday was employed as Professor of Sociology of Education at the University of Glasgow, from January 2022 to March 2023," a statement said."The Principal has commissioned a review of the appointment with the aim of understanding all the facts and learning lessons for the future."Accusations of plagiarism in Arday's work were first voiced by Nathan Cofnas - a US researcher whose role at a Cambridge college was terminated after backlash against his view that under a true meritocracy black people would "disappear from almost all high-profile positions outside of sports and entertainment".He highlighted that plagiarism detection software had found several tracts of Arday's PhD dissertation to be copied verbatim or lightly rephrased from prior academic works by other authors.Liverpool John Moores University (LJMU), which awarded Arday's PhD, has said it investigated the allegations of plagiarism last year and dismissed them, saying they were likely the result of "honest and reasonable error".It told the BBC on Friday that its position remains unchanged in light of recent events and that his PhD "still stands".Cofnas also noted that a retired professor had previously raised concerns about Arday's subsequent academic articles, which led to two journals issuing correction notes, and raised questions about some of his claimed achievements, including extensive marathon running and raising millions for charity.Several universities at which Arday claimed on his CV to have had academic positions have since denied him having those roles.The controversy has attracted a range of opinions, including within academia, about whether he had been scrutinised unfairly because of his race.Arday has admitted errors in his work but denied plagiarism, saying his autism and a lack of adequate supervision early in his academic career may have contributed to those mistakes. He also denied lying about his achievements.He said his decision to step down should not "be mistaken for an acceptance of the narratives that have surrounded me", which he has previously said were "racially motivated".Gopal said universities were "being targeted in particular by a lazy and false division between academic excellence and diversity and equality on campus", which was "really part of culture wars rather than any part of university life".She and her colleagues found it "unusual" that Arday had been appointed to a "very senior, very prestigious" post early in his career - and that he had been put forward in the media with "frankly a bit of a target on his back".Gopal also said any investigation should review "whether the university was involved in any way or any level with efforts to deter journalists from reporting on the allegations".This came after it emerged the Metropolitan Police investigated Times Higher Education (THE) reporter Jack Grove over a complaint of harassment after he contacted Arday concerning allegations of plagiarism last year.The Telegraph also reported that Arday hired law firm Carter-Ruck to send a letter to THE which implied that the "apparent attack" on Arday might be "racially motivated".The Met closed the case and Commissioner Sir Mark Rowley apologised for the investigation, telling LBC on Thursday that the complaint should have been "screened out earlier on as not requiring investigation".Great and unfortunate thingsAmong the claims by Arday that have been viewed as outlandish is one, made in an interview with the Guardian, that he was paid "1.4 million" for his memoir, Great and Unfortunate Things, due to be released next week. He did not specify the currency.While not inconceivable, publishing insiders cast doubt on a figure such as Arday being able to attract such a large advance payment.Publisher Simon & Schuster has said it plans to press ahead with the publication despite the controversy surrounding Arday.But the Atlantic reported on Thursday that there were discrepancies between an advance copy of the memoir and the proposal for the book from 2024 it had obtained.Among the differences, the magazine said the proposal gave his suicide attempt as happening before the Covid pandemic, whereas in the memoir it occurred during, and that the proposal detailed Arday being hit by a car as a teenager before "miraculously" reawakening, an episode omitted from the finished book.It comes after the Telegraph reported that Arday had claimed to have already published a book entitled Being Young, Black and Male: Challenging the Dominant Discourse.Palgrave Macmillan, which was attributed to its publication, told the newspaper it had accepted a proposal for the book but did not publish it.The BBC has contacted Simon & Schuster and the Good Law Project, which has publicly represented Arday during the plagiarism row, for comment.

schema.headline: Cambridge to review process for hiring senior academics after Jason Arday resignation

title: Officer says he's 'appalled' PC Harper's killers could be released early
description: The senior investigating officer in the PC Andrew Harper case has told BBC Breakfast he is "appalled" that two of the killers will become eligible for
body: The senior investigating officer in the PC Andrew Harper case has told BBC Breakfast he is "appalled" that two of the killers will become eligible for early release.PC Harper, 28, from Wallingford, Oxfordshire, died from catastrophic injuries in 2019 when he was dragged behind the getaway car of three teenagers who had fled the scene of a quad bike theft.Two of his killers – Jessie Cole and Albert Bowers – will be eligible for early release next year under revised government plans to tackle prison overcrowding.Stuart Blaik, who investigated the killing, said it was "particularly hard to understand" their case for early release and said police officers were shocked at the prospect.PC Harper's widow, Lissie Harper, has been among a growing number calling for Cole and Bowers to be denied early release from prison.Defence Secretary Wes Streeting told the BBC on Friday that early release is "not okay" - adding that no government should have been put in the position of having to deal with limited prison capacity.Speaking to BBC Breakfast on Friday, former Det Sup Blaik, who led the Thames Valley Police investigation, pointed to remarks by the judge who sentenced PC Harper's killers. Mr Justice Edis referred to their case of manslaughter as being "very close to a case of murder in its seriousness".The former officer called for prisoners who were judged to have had a high level of culpability for a manslaughter offence to be excluded from the scheme.Allowing them to walk free would "undermine" the judicial process and impact police morale, Blaik said, before urging the government to have a "long, hard think" about the case.The former Det Sup left Thames Valley Police in 2023. This is the first time he has publicly shared his views on the issue.Streeting said the government is taking the issue "extremely seriously"."We should never have been put in a position where prisons across the country were so full-to-bursting that any government, let alone this government, had to contemplate the early release of people from serious convictions that have led to being in prison in the first place."We're not pretending this is okay."He pointed to "strong controls" and supervision that will be in place for people released into the community and added that the government is "determined" to build more prison places and is looking carefully into the exemptions under the scheme.In an earlier statement given exclusively to BBC Breakfast, former Det Sup Blaik said "like many people across the country" he was "deeply concerned and appalled" by the prospect of Bowers and Cole being considered for early release.He said that because the "death of Andrew was such a serious and tragic case",  Bowers and Coles should "not be afforded the opportunity" to be released early."Neither of them showed any remorse during their time in police custody or during their subsequent trial."I hope the Government takes account of the strength of public feeling on this issue, which has been both clear and widespread," he added.Under revised plans announced by the government on Monday, prisoners who have committed rape, grooming, and serious child sex offences will be excluded from an early release scheme for England and Wales.But those guilty of manslaughter may still be eligible.An average of 150 people a year are sentenced at crown court for manslaughter with an average term of nine years. That means that in any given year there are hundreds of these offenders in jail. If they were all kept in, that would eat into the available spare beds - a number that is declining despite the massive prison-building programme.If the government were to try to differentiate between different types of manslaughter offenders based on the specific nature of the crime they committed, that could be legally complex to deliver - and may in turn face serious legal challenges from prisoners who find their release dates changed.Bowers and Cole were sentenced to 13 years for the manslaughter of PC Harper.They will become eligible for release from prison after serving half of their sentences under the plans, instead of two-thirds.The driver of the getaway car, Henry Long, was jailed for 16 years for the same offence. But Long will not be eligible.PC Harper and Lissie had been married for just a month when he was killed in the line of duty.On Thursday, the police officer's widow said she "will not give up" and hoped people would share a petition calling for his killers to be denied early release from prison.She said: "Hopefully we can make the current government come to their senses and realise we cannot put people like this back on our streets."Justice should mean justice and serving the sentence given."Thames Valley Police Federation chair Aileen O'Connor began the petition this week."My ask is that the prime minister, the home secretary and everybody else in government gets on the right side of this and does the right thing and makes the changes that keep the two killers behind bars," she said."We have been working closely with Chief Constable Jason Hogg and Police and Crime Commissioner Matthew Barber from the outset on this."We are all united in our frustration and dismay at the government's ridiculous plans when it comes to releasing from prison early the killers of police officers."The government said it was trying to avoid running out of prison spaces as soon as October this year.The justice secretary Alex Norris previously said about 1,000 prisoners would now not be released early following the revision to the scheme."If we drew it any wider we would have a prison capacity crisis," said Norris.Prisoners released on licence, he said, would be subject to "very significant controls on their lives" and victims would be consulted.

schema.headline: Officer says he's 'appalled' PC Harper's killers could be released early

title: Streeting 'sickened' by sex abuse claims at Army college
description: AFC is the largest military training establishment for under-19s in the UK and it receives all the Army's 16-year-old recruits.North Yorkshire Police
body: AFC is the largest military training establishment for under-19s in the UK and it receives all the Army's 16-year-old recruits.North Yorkshire Police told the BBC in a response to a Freedom of Information Act request it had received 16 reports of sexual offences linked to the college in the year to June, including allegations of exposure, voyeurism and sexual assault.No information was included on whether the reports had led to prosecutions.A total of 176 complaints of inappropriate sexual behaviour at the college were made between January 2018 and June 2025, according to Ministry of Defence (MoD) data.The women, whose names have been changed to protect their identities, all attended AFC over the last five years.One woman, Tilly, told the BBC she was 17 when she was raped at AFC by several fellow soldiers who invited her into their room."They started taking my clothes off and then this led to them doing stuff I didn't consent to."And then I was raped… by multiple junior soldiers, same age as me. It went on for hours. I felt like a piece of meat."Streeting said he sympathised with the women who had been "badly failed", and praised them for speaking up."We have a duty to uphold the very highest standards in uniform and to treat every woman with the dignity and respect she deserves."I don't want anyone who has the ambition and talent to join our armed forces to be deterred, so it's contingent on us to make sure that we've got our act together," he added.Another woman's story was shared with the BBC by her mother, who said her daughter Amy was sexually assaulted and subjected to almost daily sexual harassment during her training.Because the lock to Amy's room was not working, her mother said "she found herself sleeping across the door to stop male soldiers coming in".Another woman, who said she was sexually assaulted and harassed at AFC, described how misogynistic attitudes and behaviour of staff rubbed off on some of the male teenagers.She recalled one of the instructors saying: "It's all about the pussy and how much of it you can get."The MoD told the BBC that the college "welcomes external scrutiny and challenge".It said that AFC had in the last year "hosted the safeguarding bodies, parliamentarians, the Children's Commissioner's office and the Armed Forces Commissioner, as well as receiving an outstanding report from Ofsted".Earlier this week, Sarah Atherton, former MP for Wrexham, told the BBC that public confidence in the college could "only be restored through an independent inquiry".Atherton, who previously served in the Army's Intelligence Corps, led a 2021 government review into the experiences of women in the armed forces.Emma Lewell MP said: "If this was any other school or residential environment for children, it would have been closed down."The Children's Commissioner for England Dame Rachel de Souza said she would ensure the "appalling attacks" were investigated and "those responsible, including for failing to safeguard these girls, are held to account".She said all children living away from home had a right to contact her team for support, and that she would make sure all girls at AFC could do so.

schema.headline: Streeting 'sickened' by sex abuse claims at Army college

title: Russian drones target medics, hospitals and ambulances in Ukraine
description: Inna Lytvynenko always puts on her bright orange body armour when she's out on an emergency call.Last June, the paramedic was sent out in Kherson to t
body: Inna Lytvynenko always puts on her bright orange body armour when she's out on an emergency call.Last June, the paramedic was sent out in Kherson to treat a woman injured in a Russian drone attack, when an FPV drone smashed into her ambulance.Seconds later, she heard a buzzing sound in the sky. Another drone was flying straight towards her, fast."I panicked. I grabbed my trauma bag and started running," she recalls. "I shouted and screamed. I knew that if I stopped, I would die."After chasing her for about 10 minutes, the drone flew away. Lytvynenko was quickly picked up by police.But what she called the "safari hunting" continued. Drones hit two more vehicles that arrived to take the injured woman to hospital. Hours later, a third police car finally managed to get her out.After another "safari" attack earlier this week, Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky called to put greater pressure on Russia in order to stop deliberate "hunting attacks" on civilians.Hospitals and ambulances in Ukraine are increasingly coming under Russian drone and missile attack, even though, according to the international rules of war known as the Geneva Conventions, they must be protected by all parties to the conflict."This is a new normality, which should not be the normality," says Dr Jarno Habicht, the World Health Organization's (WHO) representative in Ukraine.The WHO has registered 3,118 attacks on healthcare since the start of the Russian invasion in February 2022. "That's two cases per day," Habicht says.Since 2023 the number of attacks on healthcare has steadily grown. In 2024 it went up by 30%. Last year there was another 20% increase. This trend is expected to continue this year.A recent Doctors Without Borders (MSF) report, external says that Russia systematically and often deliberately targets Ukrainian medical facilities. The frequency of attacks on healthcare suggests that they are "a sustained feature of the war rather than an episodic consequence of large scale offensives," the report said.Last month Russian missiles hit a hospital in Kherson, badly damaging the building and killing one doctor. Hospital director Olena Tymoshenko believes it was a targeted attack. "It wasn't just one missile, there were three missiles that hit the hospital within a few minutes from each other. It cannot be an accident," she told the BBC.Moscow also often uses a "double-tap" tactic, when they target the same location twice within a short period of time. Many believe that the second attack is deliberately aimed at first responders who arrive at the scene of the initial strike to rescue survivors.During a recent massive Russian air attack on Kyiv, seven people were killed, including a police officer and a volunteer, after a second strike on the same location.And lately Russian forces have been also targeting warehouses of humanitarian organisations. Last month alone, warehouses of three UN agencies, including the WHO, were damaged during air strikes. According to Habicht, the organisation shares coordinates of its facilities with both Moscow and Kyiv specifically in order to protect them from strikes.While missile and drone strikes can be indiscriminate, first-person view (FPV) drone strikes are almost always intentional. A drone pilot can see the target in a live feed from the drone's camera. So when it hits an ambulance, it has to be on purpose, says Robin Meldrum, MSF country coordinator in Ukraine.Dr Inna Lytvynenko says that she was wearing a uniform identifying her as a medical worker. The ambulance was also clearly marked. So, she believes the drone operator consciously chose to  target them.According to the WHO, strikes on ambulances make up 20% of all attacks on Ukraine's healthcare system, which suggests these are part of a calculated strategy.The result of such sustained attacks is that the civilian population close to the frontline are getting increasingly cut off from health services.The majority of people left in these areas are elderly people who often chronic diseases. Even if they survive air strikes and shelling, without medication and occasional check-ups they face a slow death.And ambulances may not be able to reach them if the risks are high.Lytvynenko and her colleagues constantly monitor social media to learn about threats."It's really scary," she says. "Every time when we take a patient to hospital, we just pray. These drones can appear from anywhere, they can even get through anti-drone nets."In some cases, police are dispatched instead of ambulances.Since the danger zone where FPV drones operate is growing – as both Ukraine and Russia develop drones with greater and greater ranges – mobile clinics run by various health organisations have had to shift their operations further and further away from the frontline."Two years ago, we could go up to 5-8km (3.1-5 miles) from the frontline," says Meldrum. "Now we won't go anywhere within 30km and this distance keeps growing."Over the past 18 months, MSF stopped regular visits to about 80 villages near the front where they had provided health services, says Meldrum. And recently it has paused ambulance services in Sloviansk, a major city in eastern Ukraine."It doesn't feel like we're protected in this environment, and in the way that Russia is conducting the war," Meldrum says."We don't feel that the rules of war are being respected."

schema.headline: Russian drones target medics, hospitals and ambulances in Ukraine
